title: Tages. Cipus
titleEn: Tages, and the Horns of Cipus — Metamorphoses XV.552–621
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Three wonders open this part, each only a measure of a fourth. An Etruscan ploughman watches a clod of earth stir by itself, take a man's shape and open a new mouth to speak what is coming: the people call him Tages. Romulus sees the spear fixed on the Palatine put out leaves. And Cipus, coming home victorious, catches sight of horns on his own forehead in a river. He touches them, prays that whatever they mean may fall on him rather than Rome, and sacrifices; the Etruscan seer reads the entrails and hails him king. Cipus turns his back on the walls, summons people and senate, and denounces the horned man among them without naming himself, demanding exile, chains or death. Then he lifts his wreath. The crowd groans and crowns him again, and the nobles grant him as much land as he can plough round in a day and carve his horns on the city's bronze doorposts.

sentences.t:
Et nymphas tetigit nova res, et Amazone natus
haud aliter stupuit,
sentences.l: The strange event touched the nymphs too, and the son born of the Amazon was astonished not otherwise —
sentences.i: The nymphs too were touched by the strange event, and the Amazon's son stood no less amazed —
sentences.n: The whole opening hangs on a triple comparison: “haud aliter … quam cum,” “not otherwise than when,” with three wonders following before the sentence closes. “Amazone natus,” literally “born from an Amazon,” is Hippolytus, whose mother was an Amazon queen; the ablative marks origin. “Nova res” is not news but a thing never seen before.

sentences.t:
quam cum Tyrrhenus arator
fatalem glaebam mediis adspexit in arvis
sponte sua primum nulloque agitante moveri,
sentences.l: than when the Tyrrhenian ploughman looked at the fated clod in the middle of his fields, and saw it first move of its own accord, with nothing stirring it,
sentences.i: than when the Etruscan ploughman saw the fated clod in the middle of his fields first stir of its own accord, with nothing setting it in motion,
sentences.n: “Adspexit … moveri” is a verb of seeing taking an accusative and an infinitive: he saw it move. “Nulloque agitante” is an ablative absolute — a self-contained “with no one stirring it,” where English wants a clause; you will meet this construction constantly. Tyrrhenian means Etruscan. The edition prints “adspexit” for “aspexit,” and the spelling is kept.

sentences.t:
sumere mox hominis terraeque amittere formam
oraque venturis aperire recentia fatis
sentences.l: then to take on a man's shape and to lose the earth's, and to open a mouth newly made for the fates that were coming
sentences.i: then take a man's shape and lose the earth's, and open a mouth newly made to speak the fates that were coming
sentences.n: Three more infinitives hang on the same “adspexit” as “moveri”: sumere, amittere, aperire. “Hominis … terraeque” are two genitives sharing the single noun “formam,” the shape of a man and the shape of earth. “Venturis … fatis” is dative: the new mouth is opened for the fates it is to utter.

sentences.t:
(indigenae dixere Tagen, qui primus Etruscam
edocuit gentem casus aperire futuros);
sentences.l: (the people of that country called him Tages, who first taught the Etruscan nation to open up the chances that were to come);
sentences.i: (the people of the place called him Tages — the first to teach the Etruscan nation how to lay open the chances that were to come);
sentences.n: “Dixere” is “dixerunt,” the poetic third-plural perfect in -ēre; it occurs six times in this part (dixere, Demisere, dedere, videre, imposuere, dedere). “Tagen” keeps its Greek accusative. Tages is the child who rose from the furrow and taught the Etruscans haruspicy, the reading of entrails — the art that will be practised on Cipus at 577. “Aperire” repeats the infinitive of 557, where the new mouth was opened for the fates that were coming: what Tages was given, he teaches.

sentences.t:
utve Palatinis haerentem collibus olim
cum subito vidit frondescere Romulus hastam,
sentences.l: or as when once Romulus suddenly saw the spear that stuck fast in the Palatine hills put out leaves,
sentences.i: or as when Romulus once saw, of a sudden, the spear fixed in the Palatine hills break into leaf,
sentences.n: “Utve” is “ut” with the enclitic “-ve,” “or as.” The participle “haerentem” is torn away from its noun “hastam,” which closes the line, and the reader has to hold it open across the whole clause. Behind this is the Roman story of the spear Romulus threw onto the Palatine, which took root where it landed.

sentences.l: which stood by a new root, not by the iron driven in, and now, no weapon but a tree of pliant osier, was giving unlooked-for shade to those who marvelled;
sentences.i: which stood on a new root, not on its driven point, and was a weapon no longer but a tree of supple osier, giving shade no one had looked for to the men who marvelled;
sentences.n: “Radice nova” and “ferro … adacto” are both ablatives of means, and the contrast between them is the whole point: what holds the shaft upright is no longer its rammed-in iron head but a root. “Lenti viminis” is a genitive of description, “of pliant osier.” “Admirantibus” is a participle standing on its own as a noun, in the dative: “to those marvelling.”

sentences.t:
aut sua fluminea cum vidit Cipus in unda
cornua (vidit enim)
sentences.l: or when Cipus saw his own horns in the water of the river (for he did see them)
sentences.i: or when Cipus saw his own horns in the river's water — for see them he did —
sentences.n: The third and last of the comparisons, and the one the story stays inside: the simile turns into the narrative and never comes back out. “Fluminea … in unda” is “in the river wave,” an adjective where English wants a genitive. The parenthesis “vidit enim” is the poet refusing to let the reader treat it as a trick of the light. Cipus is a Roman commander of legend, otherwise barely known; the horns are his whole story.

sentences.t:
falsamque in imagine credens
esse fidem, digitis ad frontem saepe relatis,
sentences.l: and believing the trust in the reflection to be false, with his fingers carried back to his forehead again and again,
sentences.i: and believing the reflection had lied to him, carrying his fingers back to his brow again and again,
sentences.n: “Falsam … esse fidem” is an accusative and infinitive after “credens”: he believes that the reliability in the image is false. “Fides” here is the credit one gives to a thing seen. “Digitis … relatis” is another ablative absolute, and “relatis” is from refero, to carry back — he keeps taking his hand away and putting it back.

sentences.t:
quae vidit, tetigit, nec iam sua lumina damnans
restitit, ut victor domito veniebat ab hoste,
sentences.l: he touched the things that he had seen, and no longer condemning his own eyes he halted, as he was coming victorious from an enemy he had tamed,
sentences.i: he touched what he had seen; and blaming his eyes no longer, he stopped where he stood — he was coming home a victor from a conquered enemy —
sentences.n: “Quae vidit” is a relative clause serving as the object of “tetigit”: “the things which he saw, he touched.” “Domito … ab hoste” holds the participle two words clear of its noun, with the verb and the preposition standing inside the phrase. Magnus prints “veniebat,” “was coming”; some editions print “remeabat,” “was returning.”

sentences.t:
ad caelumque manus et eodem lumina tollens
“quiquid” ait, “superi, monstro portenditur isto,
sentences.l: and lifting his hands to the sky and his eyes to the same place, “whatever,” he says, “gods above, is foretold by that portent,
sentences.i: and raising his hands to heaven and his eyes with them, “Gods above,” he said, “whatever that portent foretells,
sentences.n: “Eodem” is the adverb “to the same place,” not a form of “idem.” “Portenditur” is passive, “is foretold,” with “monstro … isto” as its ablative of means; “iste” points at the thing as something present and unwelcome. Magnus prints “quiquid” where other editions have “quicquid”; the reading is given here exactly as the edition has it. Magnus also prints “manus … lumina,” hands and eyes; some editions distribute the gesture differently, as “oculos … bracchia,” eyes and arms.

sentences.t:
seu laetum est, patriae laetum populoque Quirini,
sive minax, mihi sit!”
sentences.l: whether it is joyful — joyful let it be for my country and for the people of Quirinus — or whether it is threatening, let it be for me!”
sentences.i: if it is joyful, let the joy be my country's and Quirinus' people's; if it threatens, let it fall on me!”
sentences.n: The jussive subjunctive “sit” at the end has to serve both alternatives — the first wish has no verb of its own — while the second condition has to borrow the “est” of the first (“sive minax [est], mihi sit”). “Populo Quirini” is the Roman people, Quirinus being Romulus after his deification. The vow to take the bad half of an omen onto himself is the character of Cipus in miniature, and the rest of the tale is nothing but him carrying it out.

sentences.t:
viridique e caespite factas
placat odoratis herbosas ignibus aras
sentences.l: and altars made from green turf, grassy ones, he appeases with fragrant fires
sentences.i: and with fragrant fires he propitiates the grassy altars built of green turf
sentences.n: The narrative slips out of the perfect (“vidit,” “restitit”) into the present (“placat,” “dat,” “consulit”): the historic present, which quickens the pace at the moment of the ritual. Strictly one placates a god, not an altar; “placat aras” lets the altar stand for the power it serves. “Odoratis ignibus” are fires fed with incense.

sentences.t:
vinaque dat pateris mactatarumque bidentum,
quid sibi significent, trepidantia consulit exta.
sentences.l: and he gives wine in bowls, and consults the still-quivering entrails of the sheep that have been slaughtered, as to what they signify for him.
sentences.i: he pours wine from the bowls, and questions the still-quivering entrails of the slaughtered sheep as to what they mean for him.
sentences.n: A “bidens” is a sacrificial sheep — the word means “two-toothed,” from the age at which the animal was reckoned fit for the altar. “Quid sibi significent” is an indirect question, and it stands in front of the verb “consulit” that governs it; the reflexive “sibi” looks back to Cipus, who is asking what they signify for him. “Trepidantia” means the entrails are still moving: they are read fresh, and the trembling is part of the reading.

sentences.t:
Quae simul adspexit Tyrrhenae gentis haruspex,
magna quidem rerum molimina vidit in illis,
non manifesta tamen.
sentences.l: As soon as the diviner of the Tyrrhenian nation looked at these, he saw great strivings of things in them, not plain ones, however.
sentences.i: The moment the seer of the Etruscan nation looked at them, he saw great strivings at work in them — but nothing plain.
sentences.n: “Quae” is a connecting relative opening the sentence — “and these,” the object of “adspexit”; Latin uses a relative pronoun where English starts fresh. The “haruspex” is the entrail-reader, and he is Etruscan because Tages taught the art to the Etruscans a few lines back. “Molimina rerum” are heavings, great efforts under the surface — the seer can tell that something enormous is coming without yet being able to say what.

sentences.t:
Cum vero sustulit acre
a pecudis fibris ad Cipi cornua lumen,
sentences.l: But when he lifted his keen eye from the beast's inner parts to the horns of Cipus,
sentences.i: But when he raised his sharp gaze from the beast's entrails to Cipus' horns,
sentences.n: “Acre” closes 579 and the noun it agrees with, “lumen,” closes 580: the adjective is held a whole line away from its noun. “Lumen” is singular, the light of the eye, so “his keen sight.” “Fibrae” are the lobes and fibres of the liver, the surface a haruspex actually read.

sentences.t:
“rex” ait, “o salve! Tibi enim, tibi, Cipe, tuisque
hic locus et Latiae parebunt cornibus arces.
sentences.l: “King,” he says, “o hail! For to you, to you, Cipus, and to your horns this place and the citadels of Latium will be obedient.
sentences.i: “King,” he said, “hail to you! For it is you, Cipus — you and your horns — that this place and the citadels of Latium will obey.
sentences.n: The title comes before any explanation: he says “rex” first and names the man afterwards. “Tibi enim, tibi” doubles the pronoun for pressure. “Parebunt” takes the dative, so “tibi … tuisque cornibus” are what the citadels will obey — the horns are given a share of the kingship in their own right. “Latiae arces” means Rome and the strongholds of Latium around it.

sentences.t:
Tu modo rumpe moras portasque intrare patentes
adpropera! sic fata iubent; namque urbe receptus
rex eris et sceptro tutus potiere perenni.”
sentences.l: Only break off delay and hurry to enter the gates that stand open! so the fates command; for once received into the city you will be king, and safe you will possess an everlasting sceptre.”
sentences.i: Only break off delay, and hurry in through the open gates! The fates command it: once the city has taken you in you will be king, and secure in the mastery of a sceptre that never ends.”
sentences.n: “Rumpe moras,” literally “burst the delays,” is a set epic phrase for “waste no time.” “Potiere” is “potieris,” second singular future of the deponent potior, which takes the ablative — hence “sceptro … perenni.” “Urbe receptus” is a bare ablative where prose would want a preposition.

sentences.t:
Rettulit ille pedem torvamque a moenibus urbis
avertens faciem
sentences.l: He carried his foot back, and turning his grim face away from the walls of the city
sentences.i: He stepped back, and turning his grim face away from the city walls
sentences.n: “Rettulit pedem,” “brought his foot back,” is the ordinary Latin phrase for retreating; the doubled t is the regular form of re- plus tuli. “Torvamque” stands in the middle of 586 and “faciem” is the second word of 587: adjective and noun are split across the line-end, with the whole prepositional phrase “a moenibus urbis” between them.

sentences.t:
“procul a! procul omina” dixit
“talia di pellant! Multoque ego iustius aevum
exsul agam, quam me videant Capitolia regem!”
sentences.l: “Far off, ah, far off may the gods drive omens like these!” he said. “And much more justly will I live my life as an exile than that the Capitol should see me king!”
sentences.i: “Away — ah, far away — let the gods drive omens like these!” he said. “I shall far more justly live my life out an exile than have the Capitol look on me as king!”
sentences.n: The “a” is the interjection “ah,” not the preposition. “Di pellant” is a jussive subjunctive: a prayer, not a statement. “Multoque … iustius” is the comparative that the “quam” clause answers, and that clause takes the subjunctive “videant.” “Capitolia” is a poetic plural for the one Capitoline citadel. Magnus prints “omina,” omens; some editions print “omnia,” all things.

sentences.l: He spoke, and at once calls together the people and the weighty senate, but first he veils his horns with the laurel of peace;
sentences.i: He spoke, and at once he summons people and grave senate — but first he veils his horns in peace-bringing laurel;
sentences.n: “Dixit” is perfect and “convocat” and “velat” are present, all in one sentence: the alternation of perfect and historic present that slows and speeds the telling by turns. “Pacali lauro” — laurel was carried as a token of peace as well as of victory, so the wreath honours him and hides the horns at the same stroke.

sentences.t:
et aggeribus factis a milite forti
insistit priscosque deos e more precatus
sentences.l: and he takes his stand on a platform made by the brave soldiery, and having prayed to the gods of old after the custom
sentences.i: and takes his stand on a mound thrown up by the stout soldiery, and having prayed to the ancient gods as the custom was
sentences.n: “Insistit” governs “aggeribus” — dative or ablative, the two forms being identical. “A milite forti” is a collective singular — one “soldier” standing for the whole army — and it is the agent of “factis.” “E more” means according to established practice, the formula mattering as much as the words. “Precatus” is the participle of a deponent verb and is active in sense: “having prayed,” not “having been prayed to.”

sentences.t:
“est” ait “hic unus, quem vos nisi pellitis urbe,
rex erit. Is qui sit, signo, non nomine dicam:
cornua fronte gerit.
sentences.l: “There is,” he says, “here one man who, unless you drive him from the city, will be king. Who he is, I shall tell by a sign, not by a name: he wears horns on his forehead.
sentences.i: “There is one man here,” he said, “who will be king unless you drive him from the city. Who he is I shall tell you by a sign, not by a name: he carries horns on his brow.
sentences.n: “Quem vos nisi pellitis urbe” pulls the relative pronoun in front of the conditional clause it belongs to; English has to put the “unless” second. “Urbe” is a bare ablative of separation, “from the city.” “Is qui sit” is an indirect question. Cipus is denouncing himself, and every word of it is true.

sentences.t:
Quem vobis indicat augur,
si Romam intrarit, famularia iura daturum.
sentences.l: And the augur declares to you that he, if he shall have entered Rome, will give you the laws of household slaves.
sentences.i: And the augur declares to you that if once he enters Rome he will hand you a slave's law to live under.
sentences.n: “Quem” is another connecting relative — “and him” — and it is the accusative subject of an indirect statement whose infinitive “esse” is left out beside “daturum.” “Intrarit” is the syncopated form of “intraverit.” “Famularia iura” are the terms a household slave lives under: what he threatens them with is not merely a monarchy but servitude.

sentences.t:
Ille quidem potuit portas inrumpere apertas,
sed nos obstitimus, quamvis coniunctior illo
nemo mihi est.
sentences.l: He indeed was able to burst in through the open gates, but we stood in his way, although no one is more closely bound to me than he.
sentences.i: He could have broken in through the open gates, but we blocked him — though no one is closer to me than he is.
sentences.n: Latin says “potuit … inrumpere,” a plain perfect, where English needs “could have.” “Coniunctior illo” is a comparative with the ablative of comparison, “more joined than he.” Cipus is speaking of himself throughout in the third person, and “nos obstitimus” is his own plural: the man who blocked the gate and the man outside it are one person. Magnus keeps the unassimilated spelling “inrumpere.”

sentences.t:
Vos urbe virum prohibete, Quirites,
vel, si dignus erit, gravibus vincite catenis,
aut finite metum fatalis morte tyranni!”
sentences.l: You, Quirites, keep the man from the city, or, if he shall deserve it, bind him with heavy chains, or end your fear by the death of the fated tyrant!”
sentences.i: Keep the man out of the city, Quirites — or, if he deserves it, bind him in heavy chains, or end your fear with the death of the tyrant fate has marked!”
sentences.n: “Quirites” is the formal address to Romans assembled as citizens rather than as soldiers. “Vincite” is from vincio, to bind, not from vinco, to conquer. The three imperatives rise in severity — exclusion, chains, death — and Cipus is asking for all three against himself.

sentences.t:
Qualia succinctis, ubi trux insibilat eurus,
murmura pinetis fiunt, aut qualia fluctus
aequorei faciunt, siquis procul audiat illos,
tale sonat populus;
sentences.l: Such murmurs as arise in close-girt pine woods when the savage east wind hisses through them, or such as the waves of the sea make, if anyone should hear them from far off — with such a sound the people sounds;
sentences.i: As the murmuring that rises in close-set pinewoods when the savage east wind hisses through, or the sound the sea's waves make to a man who hears them from far off — so the crowd sounded;
sentences.n: “Qualia … aut qualia … tale” is the frame of the simile, held open across three whole lines, and the thing compared arrives at the head of 606. “Succinctis … pinetis” is dative or ablative — the two forms are identical here — and either way it puts the murmur in the woods. “Eurus” is the east or south-east wind. “Siquis” is printed as one word in this edition; “audiat” is subjunctive because the hearer is hypothetical.

sentences.t:
sed per confusa frementis
verba tamen vulgi vox eminet una “quis ille est?”,
et spectant frontes praedictaque cornua quaerunt.
sentences.l: but through the confused words of the roaring crowd one voice nevertheless stands out, “Who is that man?”, and they look at foreheads and search for the horns that were foretold.
sentences.i: yet through the jumbled words of the roaring crowd one cry nevertheless stands out — “Who is he?” — and they scan the brows around them, hunting the horns they were told of.
sentences.n: “Frementis” closes 606 and the noun it agrees with, “vulgi,” stands in the line after it: “of the roaring crowd.” “Vox … una” is a single cry lifting clear of the noise, and Ovid gives the whole crowd exactly three words of direct speech. “Praedicta” means announced beforehand — announced a moment ago, by Cipus himself.

sentences.t:
Rursus ad hos Cipus “quem poscitis” inquit, “habetis”
et dempta capiti, populo prohibente, corona
exhibuit gemino praesignia tempora cornu.
sentences.l: Again Cipus says to them, “the man you demand, you have,” and, with the garland taken from his head while the people tried to prevent it, he displayed his temples marked out by a twin horn.
sentences.i: Again Cipus says to them, “The man you are calling for, you have” — and, lifting the garland from his head though the people tried to stop him, showed his temples singled out by a pair of horns.
sentences.n: Two ablative absolutes nest here: “dempta … corona,” with the garland removed, and inside it “populo prohibente,” with the people forbidding it. “Capiti” is a dative where English says “from his head” — verse takes a thing away from a person with the dative. “Gemino … cornu” is singular in form for the pair; “praesignia” means marked out in front, distinguished.

sentences.l: All lowered their eyes and gave out a groan, and — who could believe it? — unwilling they looked at that head, famous for what it had deserved;
sentences.i: Every man dropped his eyes and gave out a groan, and — who could believe it? — looked unwillingly on that head, famous for what it had deserved;
sentences.n: Three of the poetic -ēre perfects fall together here: Demisere, dedere, videre, all standing for forms in -ērunt. “Quis credere possit” is a potential subjunctive, the poet's aside to the reader. “Meritis clarum” is an ablative: bright because of services rendered. “Inviti” is a nominative plural adjective doing an adverb's work — they were unwilling men as they looked.

sentences.t:
nec honore carere
ulterius passi, festam imposuere coronam.
sentences.l: and not having allowed it to go without its honour any longer, they set the festal garland on.
sentences.i: and, not suffering it to lack its honour any longer, they put the festal garland back.
sentences.n: “Passi” is the participle of the deponent patior and is active in sense: “having allowed.” “Carere” takes the ablative, “honore.” “Imposuere” is another of the -ērunt perfects. The crowd puts back the wreath he lifted off a few lines earlier, and in doing so refuses the one thing he had asked them for.

sentences.t:
At proceres, quoniam muros intrare vetaris,
ruris honorati tantum tibi, Cipe, dedere,
sentences.l: But the nobles, since you are forbidden to enter the walls, gave to you, Cipus, so much of honoured land
sentences.i: But the nobles, since you are forbidden to pass inside the walls, gave you, Cipus, as much honoured land
sentences.n: The poem turns and speaks to Cipus directly — “vetaris,” you are forbidden; “tibi, Cipe”; “posses,” you could. This is apostrophe, Ovid's habit of stepping out of the narrative to address a character, and it lands here on the man's reward. “Vetaris” is present passive, second singular. “Tantum” is left hanging until the “quantum” of the next line answers it.

sentences.t:
quantum depresso subiectis bubus aratro
complecti posses ad finem lucis ab ortu,
sentences.l: as you could enclose with the plough pressed down and the oxen put under the yoke, to the end of daylight from its rising,
sentences.i: as you could ring with a plough driven deep behind a yoked team, between sunrise and the day's end,
sentences.n: “Subiectis bubus,” the oxen put under the yoke, is another ablative absolute; “depresso … aratro” is the instrument you plough with, the share pressed down into the soil. “Bubus” is the ablative plural of bos; some editions print “bobus,” the same word. The Latin names the end of the day before its beginning, “ad finem lucis ab ortu.” Measuring a grant of land by what a man can plough round between sunrise and sunset is a Roman legendary form of award — and the gift is honourable and also, precisely, land outside the walls.

sentences.t:
cornuaque aeratis miram referentia formam
postibus insculpunt, longum mansura per aevum.
sentences.l: and on the bronze-plated doorposts they carve horns that give back the marvellous shape, to remain through a long age.
sentences.i: and on the bronze-clad doorposts they carve horns that give back that marvellous shape — to stand there through a long age.
sentences.n: “Referentia” is a present participle agreeing with “cornua,” bringing the shape back; “mansura” is a future participle, also with “cornua,” carrying a sense of destiny — horns that were to remain. The tale ends where Ovid's tales usually end, on a thing still standing: the doorposts of the city Cipus refused to enter now carry his horns. “Cornua” and its other cases have run through the part eight times, from the moment he first saw them in the water.
